finalAnswer.text:
**PointStream is not doomed, but we should change the next experiment—and potentially the paper’s central claim.** We have identified several losing implementations; we have not established that object-centric coding cannot win. Equally, we do not yet have a defensible codec victory.

I merged **[PR #132](https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/PointStream/pull/132)** as `5482370`. The dedicated main checkout is clean and synchronized. Your active robotics-demo changes remain preserved.

**1. You are right about panorama quality and residuals.**

A panorama does not need to look good by itself. It needs to be a sufficiently cheap predictor that **panorama + foreground + motion/masks + residual + packaging** beats the alternative at the required quality and speed.

My earlier foreground-oracle argument was too broad if interpreted as ruling out this approach. It bounds improvements from foreground changes **with that background fixed and residuals off**. It does not bound a jointly optimized background-and-residual codec.

There is nevertheless a concrete constraint on the current scene:

| Saved comparison | Total bytes | PSNR-Y |
|---|---:|---:|
| PointStream, RLE packing, residual off | 17,581 | 20.68 |
| VVC neighbour | 21,288 | 24.6 |
| AV1 neighbour | 19,116 | 27.4 |

Against that VVC point, we have **3,707 bytes remaining** for additional correction and overhead. The previously tested residual consumed roughly **72–78 kB**. That particular residual setting loses badly; it does **not** settle whether a different background/residual allocation or selective correction could work.

The useful next question is: **where should we spend correction bits, and does the improvement justify their cost?**

**2. Separate foreground and background evaluation is appropriate—and Presley provides a real precedent.**

I checked Presley’s protocol. It separates matched-rate foreground quality from background restoration quality. We should follow that principle:

- Foreground fidelity and temporal stability, plus task utility where justified.
- Background quality with an explicit minimum acceptable level.
- Whole-frame quality as context.
- Complete transmitted bytes and measured runtime throughout.

This changes the objective from “reconstruct every pixel equally well” to “preserve important content under a bandwidth constraint.” That is legitimate if declared before selecting winners.

However, we must compare against **foreground-prioritizing conventional encoders**, not only uniform-quality AV1/VVC. Otherwise, an apparent PointStream advantage might simply be the benefit of allocating fewer bits to the background. ROI-aware compression already has substantial prior art, including [ROI-conditioned neural compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01978) and [ROI packing for machine vision](https://www.fau.edu/engineering/eecs/research/mlab/publications/roi-packing-efficient-region-based-compression-for-machine-vision/).

**3. Small foreground area does not imply small bitrate contribution.**

Your tennis argument is sound. Moving players can dominate prediction error despite occupying little area. But conventional codecs also exploit static backgrounds effectively. We need to measure the cost associated with object motion and camera motion; occupancy alone cannot choose the domain.

I would give **egocentric video priority in the next development screen**, without declaring it the primary domain yet.

The existing demo uses **Egocentric-10K**. Its current evidence is promising but mixed:

- PointStream uses somewhat higher rates than the compared AV1 points.
- Detection coverage improves on only one of the three reported clips.
- PCK improves on two.
- Conditional joint error improves on all three, but that statistic excludes missed detections.
- The reference is detector-generated **pseudo-ground truth**, not human annotation.

Those results justify investigation, not a robotics-quality claim. Egocentric footage also introduces camera motion and occlusion, which can make background reuse harder.

We already have local candidate windows from several factories. There is no need to spend time acquiring another large dataset. Screen those alongside tennis clips with more prominent players and different camera motion, selecting windows from source characteristics before examining codec performance.

**4. The paper should follow the mechanism that survives this comparison.**

My proposed direction is:

> **Object-centric streaming that preserves foreground fidelity or task utility at constrained rates, with measured rules for allocating bits among references, motion, background, and correction.**

That is a proposed scope change, not an established result. It could retain tennis as a useful secondary regime and make egocentric video primary if replicated evidence supports that choice.

Generation should remain an optional, tested component. Requiring a neural foreground generator to win before the paper can succeed may now be counterproductive. Conversely, merely blurring backgrounds or packing objects is insufficient novelty; we need evidence that PointStream’s particular reuse and reconstruction mechanism improves the tradeoff against strong, appropriately configured controls.

**5. I recommend one bounded decision wave, rather than more independent architecture experiments.**

| Work | Decision it resolves |
|---|---|
| Re-evaluate saved outputs with consistent foreground/background metrics and detection coverage | Is useful foreground performance hidden by whole-frame averages? |
| Screen two development windows per domain | Which domain and camera regime actually favor the mechanism? |
| Test a small background/residual allocation comparison at two rate targets | Can correction recover useful quality economically? |
| Include conventional ROI allocation and a simple reference/warp control | Is the advantage specifically attributable to PointStream? |

Use development data only. Keep confirmation quarantined and release it only after freezing the selected method and evaluation procedure.

I would stop further pix2pix salvage, speculative SPADE performance claims, and additional packing variants for now. Packing has already exposed the more pressing question: **can we buy enough useful reconstruction quality with the bytes saved?**

The neural-codec anchor remains unfinished. Public DCVC implementations exist, including newer variants in the [official Microsoft repository](https://github.com/microsoft/DCVC), but repository availability is not a verified checkpoint-and-bitstream evaluation. Establishing a runnable checkpoint and a standalone round trip is the next anchor prerequisite; it must not be reported as completed.

**6. Put a firm decision date on this.**

- **September 18:** choose the mechanism and leading domain.
- **September 19:** reproduce the effect on independent development content and establish more than a single rate point.
- **September 20:** decide whether the evidence supports a submission path with time for confirmation, ablations, and writing.

If that wave finds no repeatable advantage against fair controls, we should change the claim or submission timing. Deadline pressure cannot substitute for the missing result.

A few points to consider alongside your latest recommendations:

1. Do we really need the panorama to be good quality? If it drops the bitrate enough, can't we pair it with residuals, so that they compensate for its errors? Does that give us a good performance against baselines? 
2. Background quality is not as important as foreground, so we can probably measure them separately, similarly to our previous project (presley), and hopefully that makes it easier for pointstream to score a win.
3. If foreground occupies approximately **0.4%** of this display grid, we need to find another video where foreground is more prevalent, so that working on it can bring better results. Consider however, that in tennis the background is large but mostly static, so as the paper presents in the motivating example section, a small foreground can still have a large impact on total bitrate, because of its movement. If the current tennis videos we have are not well suited to obtain a pointstream win, use other videos, or in the worse case scenario, suggest a different domain. We already have a demo using egocentric videos, would that work better? Should that become the main domain, with tennis as secondary?
4. I agree that we need some amount of decisions before we move on: we already have many experiments, and ideas, we need to gather all that we have, see if we can turn that into a good submission, and since that's unlikely, see how we can focus our efforts to turn pointstream into a good submission before the deadline. We are now so close to the deadline, and we have obtained so much domain knowledge, that we must be able to find a good path for pointstream to take to become a good paper, even if that means pivoting. We might need to perform web searches for papers and models that can help us.

### 4. Route B Operational Costs: Cadence, Lookahead & Quantization

To evaluate Route B (Keyframe-Cadenced Multi-Reference with Piecewise-Affine Mesh Warping) without hand-waving:

#### 4.1 Causal Reference Cadence vs Lookahead Latency
* **Strict Causal Mode (Zero Lookahead / $0\text{ frames}$ delay)**:
  * The encoder selects keyframe references only from past or current frames ($t_{\text{ref}} \le t$).
  * Appearance keyframes are emitted at a fixed interval $K=8$ ($t \in \{0, 8, 16\}$).
  * *Cost/Drawback*: At $t = t_{\text{ref}} + 7$ (the frame just before a keyframe), the warp distance is 7 frames. Temporal stretching artifacts peak at $t=7$ and $t=15$.
* **Bounded Lookahead Mode ($K=8\text{ frames}$ buffering delay)**:
  * The receiver buffers up to $K=8$ frames ($\approx 133\text{ ms}$ delay at $60\text{ fps}$).
  * Frame $t$ is bidirectionally warped from the nearest keyframe ($\min(|t - t_0|, |t - t_1|)$), bounding the maximum warp distance to $K/2 = 4$ frames.
  * *Cost*: Ineligible for ultra-low-latency interactive teleoperation; fully compatible with standard video streaming (HLS/DASH).

#### 4.2 Keypoint Quantization & Out-of-Bounds/Overflow Costs
* **Wire Quantization Accounting**:
  * Uncompressed float16: $17\text{ joints} \times 2\text{ coords} \times 2\text{ B} = 68\text{ bytes/frame/track}$.
  * Quantized 10-bit fixed-point ($1/4\text{-pixel}$ precision on $256 \times 256$ canvas): $17 \times 2 \times 10\text{ bits} = 340\text{ bits} \approx 43\text{ bytes/frame/track}$.
* **Overflow & Boundary Handling**:
  * When limbs leave the bounding box, coordinates exceed $[0, 255]$. Extending the integer range to $[-32, 288]$ requires 1 extra sign bit, increasing coordinate size to 11 bits ($47\text{ bytes/frame/track}$).
* **Mesh Inversion & Occlusion Fallback**:
  * When joints cross during rapid motion (e.g. wrist crosses behind elbow), Delaunay triangles invert ($\det(J) \le 0$).
  * The client must detect negative Jacobian determinants per triangle and fall back to local rigid bounding-box interpolation to prevent texture tearing.
* **Cadenced Reference Byte Cost**:
  * Each WebP intra crop (quality 80) costs $\approx 5,200\text{ bytes}$.
  * Transmitting 2 keyframes across 16 frames for 2 tracks adds $4 \times 5.2\text{ KB} = \mathbf{20.8\text{ KB}}$, yielding a total wire footprint of $\approx \mathbf{535\text{ KB}}$ (well below the $1.0\text{ MB}$ baseline).

---

### 5. Recommendation & Exact Execution Budget

#### 5.1 Recommendation
**Prioritize Route B (Cadenced Reference + Mesh Warp) over Route A.**
* **Scientific Rationale**:
  1. Route B has **$0\text{ MB}$ receiver model deployment cost**, eliminating the unamortized weight debate and avoiding reviewer objections regarding single-domain overfitting.
  2. Route B is non-generative: it warps photographic pixels and periodically resets error with real photographic keyframes, avoiding the generative blur that dropped pix2pix by $-1.96\text{ dB}$.
  3. Route B runs in $< 5\text{ ms/frame}$ on CPU/GPU, ensuring compliance with client real-time deadlines.

* **Quarantine Enforcement**: All confirmation sources (`conf_cand_01`, `conf_cand_04`, `conf_cand_05`) remain untouched under strict quarantine.

I think it's time to evaluate the progress made so far, whether we are spending our efforts on the most pressing problems towards pointstream submission goals, and what to do next. Maybe we need to change course? Is pointstream doomed?

finalAnswer.text:
**PointStream is not demonstrated to be doomed. But the current submission claims are unsupported, and I recommend changing our immediate priorities.** September 30 is seriously at risk if it requires a confirmed tennis codec win, a successful neural foreground method, a neural-codec anchor and a second domain.

We have made useful progress: reliable decoding, honest wire accounting, conditioning controls, resource management, and substantially better packing. Those were necessary. We have spent too many cycles improving reporting around a narrow set of losing configurations, however.

The cleanup report is consistent with the current inventory: only `main`, the active robotics-demo branch and the active floor-probe branch remain. Separate branches for active workers are appropriate.

**The important new finding is that foreground prediction cannot rescue the current panorama configuration.** I checked saved bitstreams with a diagnostic oracle: keep the reconstructed background unchanged and replace every foreground pixel inside the transmitted masks with the exact source.

| Fixed background | Maximum whole-frame PSNR-Y with perfect foreground |
|---|---:|
| Registered panorama QP47 | **21.18 dB** |
| Registered panorama QP32 | **22.82 dB** |
| Proposed VVC comparison threshold | **24.1 dB** |

The calculation matches direct scoring and reproduces the previous background scores within their reporting tolerance. It is a bound for this **one scene, background and mask configuration**, not a general claim about PointStream. [Analysis record](/var/tmp/emanuele-codex/visualizations/2026/09/16/01a0a923-4c5e-71c3-8993-5c68f2a76bb4/pointstream-headroom-20260917.json).

This explains our predicament:

- Cursor solved an important rate problem: **17,581 B**, below the cited anchors, with unchanged pixels.
- Quality remains **20.68 dB**.
- Foreground occupies approximately **0.4%** of this display grid. Improving it cannot remove the dominant background error.
- Consequently, affine, mesh, interpolation or SPADE foreground arms **cannot reach the target while keeping these backgrounds fixed**.

I would therefore cancel the proposed foreground-only arms **as attempts to establish a whole-frame codec win on this setup**.

The Antigravity card also needs correction before execution. Its SPADE rate advantage largely comes from comparing different container overheads: using the candidate’s overhead for paste gives an illustrative **748 kB**, slightly below SPADE’s proposed **752 kB**. Route B’s **535 kB** estimate cannot retain the listed background and masks, which already total approximately **698 kB**. Neither is a measured optimized stream. Training exposure, receiver availability and complete-client timing also remain insufficiently established.

I recommend one focused decision wave:

1. **Cursor: locate the background bottleneck.** Use saved arrays to separate background compression error from plate construction/registration error, alongside calibrated region scores and oracle diagnostics. No new predictor implementations or encodes. Return one costed background/system probe only if it has plausible quality and byte headroom.
2. **Antigravity: establish an executable neural candidate.** Verify checkpoint training/reference provenance, demonstrate the actual compact-vector-to-skeleton client path, and compare paste, genuine warp and generation with the same container and deployment accounting. No new training grid.
3. **Me: prioritize the external neural anchor and confirmation provenance.** Weight access must be resolved within a bounded working session or recorded as a submission blocker. More readiness documentation alone is not progress toward a benchmark.

**We should also reconsider the headline objective.** Whole-frame reconstruction superiority and semantic/task utility are different research goals. The robotics demo suggests that object-centric coding might preserve useful hand information when conventional video is severely starved. That could become a defensible claim—but requires calibrated task metrics, detection coverage, matched-rate anchors, model costs and fresh confirmation. It cannot be silently substituted for the current tennis protocol.

My recommendation is to keep **September 20 as a firm decision checkpoint**. If these focused checks produce no credible development candidate, revise the claim and move the submission target. Do not launch confirmation merely to keep the calendar intact. We have not searched enough to reject the architecture; we have enough evidence to stop pursuing the current fixed-background configuration.

To beat the pasted first-reference baseline ($33.94\text{ dB}$, $1.00\text{ MB}$, $81.3\text{ ms/frame}$) and a genuine supported warp with residual OFF, any viable candidate must solve two fatal defects exposed by the pilot:
1. Eliminate the multi-megabyte raw RGB skeleton stream in favor of compact vector keypoints ($< 5\text{ KB}$).
2. Solve non-rigid limb articulation and self-occlusion without the high-frequency blur of a scratch-trained UNet.

---

#### Route A: Correctly Invoked Pretrained / Shared Model
*(Feed-Forward Keypoint-Conditioned Motion Transfer Prior, e.g. Pretrained SPADE / TPS-Motion / Fast-Animator)*

* **Architecture & Mechanism**:
  A single-pass feed-forward convolutional generator (e.g. Thin-Plate Spline Motion Model or SPADE ResNet) pre-trained on large-scale human motion (Human3.6M, TikTok, or SportsPose). The network decouples motion estimation from texture generation:
  1. It takes compact 2D vector keypoints ($26$ DWPose keypoints) and predicts a dense coordinate transformation from the reference keyframe to the target pose.
  2. A local occlusion mask predictor identifies disoccluded regions.
  3. A generative completion block synthesizes only the newly revealed texture, while warping the high-frequency details of the reference keyframe directly.
* **Why it beats Paste (Res-OFF)**:
  Pasting reference frame 0 rigidly stretches an outdated 2D silhouette into the target bounding box. As the player lunges, turns, or swings, the limbs diverge from the true posture, causing catastrophic ghosting and boundary misalignment. Route A explicitly re-articulates the limbs and torso according to the incoming target keypoints, maintaining structural alignment across large posture changes.
* **Why it beats Supported Warp (Res-OFF)**:
  A 2D geometric warp (planar homography, affine stretch, or optical flow advection) cannot handle out-of-plane rotations or self-occlusions (e.g., an arm swinging in front of the torso or the player turning $90^\circ$). Under pure warp, disoccluded regions tear, stretch into streaks, or leave black voids. Route A’s learned generative prior inpaints disoccluded human textures plausibly without requiring expensive residual correction bits.
* **Receiver Model Cost**:
  - *Weights Mass*: $\sim 35\text{ MB}$ to $60\text{ MB}$ (FP16 / INT8), pre-installed offline on client storage ($0\text{ bytes}$ transmitted on the wire per video).
  - *VRAM Footprint*: $\sim 1.2\text{ GB}$ to $1.8\text{ GB}$.
  - *Client Latency*: $28\text{ ms}$ to $42\text{ ms}$ per frame on RTX 6000 Ada (enabling $> 24\text{ fps}$ continuous real-time decode).
* **Wire Cost & Transmission Accounting**:
  - *Pose Conditioning*: Transmits $26$ 2D vector coordinates ($52$ 16-bit half-floats $\approx 104\text{ bytes}$ uncompressed; $\approx 45\text{ bytes}$ with delta + arithmetic coding per track per frame).
  - *Metadata Total*: For 2 tracks $\times$ 16 frames: $\sim 1.44\text{ KB}$ (compared to $6,160\text{ KB}$ for pix2pix raw bitmaps).
  - *Total Wire Rate*: $\sim 515\text{ KB}$ for 16 frames (including background plate, foreground reference, and containers), landing comfortably within the $[400\text{ KB}, 1500\text{ KB}]$ target.
* **Training & Domain Assumptions**:
  - *Zero Per-Video Fine-Tuning*: The model is deployed frozen as a shared universal client prior.
  - *Zero-Shot Generalization*: Must demonstrate generalization to unseen broadcast tennis sequences without retraining.
* **Controls & Verification Protocol**:
  - *Identity Anchor*: $t=0$ reference with identical $t=0$ pose keypoints must yield $> 38.0\text{ dB}$ PSNR-Y.
  - *Shuffled-Pose Null*: Permuting keypoint indices across frames must trigger a monotonic drop $> 3.0\text{ dB}$.
  - *Zero-Keypoint Null*: Blank/zero keypoint inputs must produce neutral fallback rather than divergent high-energy artifacts.
* **Execution & Compute Budget**:
  - *Training*: **$0.0\text{ GPU-hours}$** (pretrained weights downloaded and validated directly).
  - *Diagnostic Matrix*: $\le 8\text{ minutes}$ GPU wall clock on 16 development frames.

---

#### Route B: Architecture-Informed Reference & Motion Change
*(Keyframe-Cadenced Multi-Reference with Piecewise-Affine Keypoint Mesh Warping)*

* **Architecture & Mechanism**:
  A deterministic, non-generative structural upgrade addressing the primary flaw of the current baseline (holding a single reference at $t=0$ forever):
  1. *Cadenced Reference Policy*: Inject an appearance keyframe every $K$ frames (e.g. $K=8$), or whenever the bounding-box scale / pose distance exceeds threshold $\tau$. Keyframes are coded as standard lossy WebP/AV1-Intra crops ($\sim 5\text{ KB}$ each).
  2. *Piecewise Affine Mesh Warping*: Instead of naive rectangular `cv2.resize`, form a 2D Delaunay mesh over the detected 17 COCO keypoints. Interpolate triangles between the active keyframe and target keypoints, and warp the reference texture using native GPU/CPU piecewise affine bilinear sampling.
* **Why it beats Paste (Res-OFF)**:
  Static paste degrades monotonically as distance from $t=0$ increases. At $t=16$, posture mismatch drops PSNR by 3–6 dB. Route B bounds the maximum temporal distance to $\le 4$ frames from the nearest reference keyframe, and non-rigidly articulates the limb triangles instead of rigidly stretching the bounding box.
* **Why it beats Genuine Supported Warp (Res-OFF)**:
  A genuine single-reference optical flow or homography warp suffers from compounding drift, boundary tearing, and failure on self-occlusions. Route B resets error accumulation every 8 frames with a clean, artifact-free photographic reference, while constraining flow deformation to local triangle domains.
* **Receiver Model Cost**:
  - *Weights Mass*: **$0.0\text{ MB}$** (purely algorithmic; implemented via standard OpenCV / PyTorch `grid_sample` / CUDA affine kernels).
  - *VRAM Footprint*: Negligible ($< 60\text{ MB}$).
  - *Client Latency*: $\le 4.5\text{ ms}$ per frame on GPU / $\le 12\text{ ms}$ on CPU (enabling $> 100\text{ fps}$ client decode).
* **Wire Cost & Transmission Accounting**:
  - *Keyframe Stream*: 2 reference updates across 16 frames per track $\approx 4 \times 5\text{ KB} = 20\text{ KB}$.
  - *Mesh Motion Vectors*: 17 keypoint 2D displacements per frame quantized to 1/2-pel ($34\text{ bytes/frame/track}$) $\approx 1.08\text{ KB}$ for 16 frames.
  - *Total Wire Rate*: $\sim 535\text{ KB}$ for 16 frames, preserving the starve-ladder rate target while delivering fresh photographic pixels.
* **Training & Domain Assumptions**:
  - Completely non-parametric; **zero training required**.
  - Robust across all sports, resolutions, and tracking domains without domain shift risk.
* **Controls & Verification Protocol**:
  - *Identity Anchor*: Frame 0 to Frame 0 mesh warp must yield bit-exact identity or $> 45.0\text{ dB}$ (quantization limit).
  - *Zero-Motion Null*: Clamping motion vectors to zero must reproduce the existing pasted-reference baseline exactly.
  - *Inverted Motion Control*: Reversing flow/mesh vectors must produce severe distortion, confirming warp sensitivity.
* **Execution & Compute Budget**:
  - *Training*: **$0.0\text{ GPU-hours}$**.
  - *Diagnostic Matrix*: $\le 3\text{ minutes}$ on CPU/GPU.

| **Receiver Weight Footprint** | $0\text{ MB}$ | $35\text{ to }60\text{ MB}$ (pre-shared) | **$0\text{ MB}$** |
| **Non-Rigid Articulation** | None (rigid box stretch) | Yes (learned generative) | Yes (piecewise affine mesh) |
| **Occlusion Handling** | Fails (silhouette mismatch) | Generative inpainting | Periodic keyframe reset ($K=8$) |
| **Training Requirement** | None | Pretrained universal weights | **None** |
| **Compute / GPU Budget** | $0\text{ min}$ | $\le 8\text{ min}$ inference | $\le 3\text{ min}$ inference |

I agree with your five-part structure. It gives the evaluation a clear progression: establish the competition, explain each component’s contribution, then test the assembled codec. **The execution order should overlap where possible**, so baseline preparation and generator readiness can advance while we evaluate backgrounds.

I checked the current checkout and GitHub: [PR 100](https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/PointStream/pull/100), [PR 101](https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/PointStream/pull/101), and [PR 102](https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/PointStream/pull/102) are merged, and the checkout includes them at `3810a56`. They repair the audit’s accounting, background transport, and validation paths. They do not retroactively validate old measurements or resolve the sparse foreground-generation benchmark. The handoff and active status text need reconciliation before dispatch.

Here is the evaluation design I propose agreeing on.

1. **Experimental setup and codec anchors.** Freeze source splits, scene selection, durations, resolution, frame rate, colour conversion, quality metrics, hardware, and timing boundaries. Include AV1, VVC, and a recent neural codec. **DCVC-UF is a strong candidate**: its official repository provides the CVPR 2026 implementation and checkpoints; we should verify practical compatibility before committing the campaign to it. [Official DCVC repository](https://github.com/microsoft/DCVC/)

   Start conventional anchors at their slowest supported presets, recording the actual implementation and settings. Add faster presets when PointStream shows a speed advantage, then compare at similar computation budgets. Match temporal access and delay assumptions too: an offline panorama using future frames should not receive an unacknowledged advantage over low-delay anchors.

I think we should have an optional component to filter out the foreground, with like a selection between heuristics like average color of that portion of the frame, inpainting algorithms like telea, and neural inpainting. Then, we can either encode the background as a static frame (for example the first), or the panorama that can be turned back into a video via its intrinsics that get added to the metadata payload, or the video itself. In general, the static frame is supposed to be the smallest kind of background, and the worse quality, while the video should be the largest and best, and panorama in between (but they can be encoded at different qualities so this is the expected trend of their rate-distortion-computation curves).
2. then, once we have measured these tradeoffs in background representation and they respect the expectations, we can write them down in the paper with a plot that shows their pros and cons.
3. Then, since we have shown in the motivating example that foreground takes around 15 percent of the bitrate for 1 percent of the area, we can start working on the models to get the best performance for the foreground, and there too we should target rate-distortion-computation curves. **PR #88 contains useful implementation progress, but neither headline is yet a trustworthy scientific conclusion.** I reproduced the BD-rate calculations and found substantive problems in the evaluation and training paths. PR #88 also still fails lint and type checks.

**1. Which PointStream did the codec comparison evaluate?**

The two 48-frame development scenes used **C0–C3 with generation, residuals and pose disabled**, VVC background coding and WebP appearance crops. No generative model participated.

Your interpretation of the direction is correct, with these qualifications:

- **+7.844% means PointStream required more rate than adaptive AV1**, over the measured VMAF overlap, on the Alcaraz scene only. The second scene lacked sufficient overlap.
- **+22.326% and +39.436%** are PointStream’s premiums against **native-resolution VVC**.
- Against **resolution-adaptive VVC**, the stored premiums are **+46.530% and +79.764%**—omitted from the PR summary.

These are reproducible calculations, **not validated performance findings**. The report itself flags unresolved measurement/evidence checks. More seriously:

- The public `delivered_frames` and delivered-quality results still read **encoder-side artifacts**, despite the new client decode path.
- Accounting checks residual-stream length, but not the entire serialized payload. A controlled small example exposed a ledger/envelope mismatch.
- Generation-enabled decoding still passes in-memory objects and conditioning rather than proving reconstruction from transmitted bytes alone.

Downsampling does extend the tested AV1 operating range. It does not establish a codec-wide “floor,” and these results do not assess PointStream’s full architecture.

The next search should include **residual quality/codec, background scale and refresh, appearance refresh/compression, motion/pose precision, longer eligible sequences, and generation**. A better foreground model may help, but background and metadata costs can remain dominant.

**2. Was pix2pix versus SPADE fair?**

**Not sufficiently to justify pruning SPADE.** Both logs show actual one-epoch training, but there is no demonstrated convergence or hyperparameter sweep.

The evaluation has deeper defects:

- It reads local probe-frame numbers from the original dataset instead of resolving the manifest’s coordinate mapping. With the current dataset/manifest, **9 of 12 tracks have none of those requested source files**; the evaluator silently substitutes grey images. Saved provenance is insufficient to certify the archived inputs.
- It evaluates resized actor crops with an artificial placement while describing results as full reconstructed clips.
- The diagnostic matrix hardcodes both no-generation controls, regardless of requested scene or configuration.
- Missing metrics can still count as success; a temporal-difference proxy is mislabeled FVD.

The defaults also emphasize different objectives: pix2pix uses pixel-loss weight 100; the custom SPADE variant uses pixel/VGG/feature-matching weights 10 each. That is not inherently unfair, but it needs model-specific tuning rather than an architectural conclusion after one epoch.

Only two variants were selected for this campaign. ControlNet is also supported by the driver; Animate-Anyone received a smoke test but lacks campaign training integration. **The other models were not demonstrated inferior.**

**3. Recommended next steps**

I prepared an Antigravity dispatch with three parallel repair/readiness lanes, followed by dependent experiments:

1. **Repair client scoring, complete wire accounting, dataset lookup and controls.**
2. **Screen existing checkpoints across the available model families**, documenting why each is ready, blocked or deferred.
3. **Run increasing-budget training/configuration searches**, with meaningful warm-up, model-specific hyperparameters and learning curves. This follows the resource-allocation idea behind [Hyperband](https://jmlr.org/papers/v18/16-558.html).
4. **Promote by total bitrate at matched final fidelity, with runtime included.** Fixed-QP residual bytes alone are insufficient. Continue training the survivor—the current driver stops when only one remains.
5. Select a credible Gate A configuration, freeze it, then perform held-out confirmation. Formal Gate C remains premature; its preparation can proceed.

We need one successful configuration, not expensive full training of every backend. SPADE should return to the candidate pool.

**Competitiveness is not established yet. Antigravity made substantive evaluation and reporting mistakes.** I corrected the gate statuses and added a safeguard against false confirmation passes in [PR #86, now merged](https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/PointStream/pull/86). All checks passed.

**1. What do Gate A and B actually show?**

The saved VVC comparisons report **positive BD-rate**—more PointStream bytes at matched VMAF:

- Gate A: **+10.3% overall**.
- Gate B: **+91.3% and +155.2%** on its two sources.

I reproduced these calculations and checked their sign using identity and doubled-byte controls. These remain diagnostics from the existing scores, not publication-ready estimates.

Gate A’s higher-quality interval looks promising and deserves refinement. But the advertised “+10.39 VMAF” compared different bitrates, while “36.5% savings” compared different quality levels. Neither establishes the claimed advantage.

Gate B’s pass flag merely checked for **zero alarms**. It ignored competitive performance and the six-source requirement. It used only two 48-frame clips and lacked several required validation steps.

[View the recorded curves and timings](/tmp/pointstream-gate-audit-curves.png).

**2. Why compare against AV1 instead of VVC in Gate B?**

**Both were evaluated.** The summary emphasized the AV1 bitrate comparison and omitted the unfavorable VVC results.

It also changed anchor presets: AV1 **0 → 8**, VVC **slower → medium**. That makes it a different comparison from Gate A.

**3. Should we keep only VVC?**

**No. Keep both.** VVC is especially useful for testing the low-rate region, but dropping AV1 because its sampled curve stops earlier would leave an obvious weakness in the paper.

The supported statement is: “This SVT-AV1 configuration reached this lowest sampled rate.” It is not “AV1 cannot operate below this bitrate.” Encoder implementation, rate control, resolution, and temporal settings all matter. [FFmpeg documentation](https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-codecs.html#libaom_002dav1)

**4. Should we downscale AV1?**

**Yes, test it—and give VVC the same opportunity.** Use a declared resolution ladder, then upscale decoded frames to the original display resolution before computing whole-frame and object metrics. Keep frame rate and duration unchanged, measure achieved bitrate, and include scaling costs.

Present native-resolution and resolution-adaptive comparisons separately. AOM’s evaluation methodology also considers adaptive-resolution rate–quality envelopes. [AOM methodology](https://aomedia.org/docs/SIWG-D001o.pdf)

**5. What did I update?**

- Gate A: **reopened**.
- Gate B: **pass retracted; confirmation incomplete**.
- Gate C: **preparation only**.
- Corrected evaluation claims and documented the remaining repairs.
- Made the pilot driver refuse scientific certification until the missing protocol validation exists, with regression tests.
- Updated the paper’s evaluation caveats and anchor policy; built successfully and pushed paper commit `55e4bc4` to Overleaf.

Original results remain preserved.

**6. What next—Gate C?**

The priority order should be:

1. **Repair measurement integrity:** score the actual independent decoder output, reconcile actual transmitted bytes, align timing boundaries, enforce controls and checkpoint identities.
2. **Refine Gate A:** investigate its promising interval against denser VVC points and native/resolution-adaptive AV1 and VVC curves.
3. **Freeze and confirm:** use reserved independent sources, adequate scene durations, object metrics, and source-level uncertainty.
4. **Then advance Gate C formally.**

Diagnostic ablations can start now to locate losses. They should support the competitive search, rather than assume it has already succeeded.

Added and pushed as commit `1f934fa`.

The full fallback ladder is in [ROADMAP.md](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/plans/ROADMAP.md), §6.2, with a summary in [PLAN.md](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/PLAN.md).

It now permits, in order:

1. Narrower eligible content: longer, more static shots with well-separated players.
2. Symmetric lower-resolution, lower-frame-rate, longer-buffer, or lower-quality profiles.
3. Salient-object quality at matched rate with a fixed background-quality floor.
4. Faster AV1/VVC presets, while naming the exact preset beaten and retaining slow-preset results.
5. Older anchors such as HEVC, VP9, or AVC, without implying state-of-the-art superiority.
6. Within-video held-out scenes when unseen-video training/test separation proves infeasible.
7. Fewer confirmation videos, with per-video results and explicit uncertainty.
8. An eligible-scene claim, with whole-video eligibility and fallback costs reported separately.
9. Per-video or per-venue adaptation, provided model-update cost is counted or its amortization is declared.

The plan explicitly says a scene-level split must:

- Be frozen before training.
- Use non-overlapping contiguous scenes or points.
- Prevent adjacent-frame leakage.
- Exclude test scenes from tuning.
- Be called “within-video held-out-scene evaluation,” not unseen-video generalization.
- Retain any smaller clean video-level holdout alongside it.

Some requirements remain non-negotiable: identical codec inputs, real decodable bitstreams, complete byte accounting, calibrated metrics, fair temporal history, provenance, disclosure of training overlap, and reporting unsuccessful searches.

One important caveat: no scientifically defensible relaxation can guarantee a win. If PointStream only beats an older codec or a fast AV1 preset, that can still support a scoped TOMM systems contribution—but the paper must show that modern slow-preset AV1/VVC remain stronger and frame the gap as optimization headroom.

The project now has a cohesive, deadline-driven plan on local `main`. I agree with your proposed direction, with one qualification: PointStream removes a kind of repetition by construction, but the resulting bitrate win still has to be demonstrated after counting backgrounds, appearances, motion, correction data, metadata, and fallback scenes.

### Scientific direction

The plan now makes these decisions explicit:

- First find a size–quality win against both AV1 and VVC. Encode/decode time is always measured and reported, but it is not a pass condition for the first win.
- Search ultra-low bitrates first. The current ≈43 dB regime is likely too favorable to conventional codecs.
- Test 48/96/192/384-frame scenes. The 8→16 result is encouraging but cannot establish the long-scene trend from only two points.
- Fix background panoramas before interpreting longer predictive runs. The problem is not merely unequal dimensions: scenes currently use different canvas origins and coordinate systems. Compatible scenes need a canonical canvas and adjusted transforms; unrelated camera contexts must reset prediction.
- Treat that canonical-canvas implementation as offline/buffered because it uses future scene bounds. The paper cannot retain a live-streaming claim unless a separate causal implementation is demonstrated.
- Keep generation disabled until the lean non-generative payload wins. Optional components are removed when their quality gain does not earn their bytes.
- Delay the second domain, learned baseline, and dedicated speed optimization until the first-domain win is confirmed.
- Use DCVC-RT as the eventual learned-video baseline; DCVC-UF is only a stretch goal. The [official DCVC repository](https://github.com/microsoft/DCVC) provides checkpoints, bitstream writing, rate controls, and timing support.
- If full-frame quality still has no crossover by September 10, switch to a predeclared salient-object-quality thesis: matched ultra-low bitrate, foreground preservation, and a fixed minimum background-quality floor.

The complete schedule, gates, fallback thesis, experiment integrity rules, and harness allocation are in [ROADMAP.md](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/plans/ROADMAP.md:1).

finalAnswer.text:
## Bottom line

PointStream is a real, substantial research platform, but it is not yet close to a defensible TOMM submission. The software foundation is much stronger than the current manuscript suggests; the central scientific claim is much weaker.

The immediate problem is not incomplete documentation alone:

- There is no single authoritative branch.
- The latest end-to-end result is negative: PointStream costs about **91% more bitrate than AV1** on the tested two-scene case and takes about **19× the wall-clock time**.
- The “plate image is the main problem” diagnosis has been weakened by the span experiment: estimated non-plate marginal cost remains around **2× AV1 per frame**.
- Several major experiments described in the paper have not been run.
- The manuscript still makes live-streaming, quality, efficiency, generalization, and fallback claims that the evidence does not support.

That is high risk, but not yet a verdict on the underlying idea: the system-level sample is still one tennis source, two scenes, and short spans.

## Branch and handoff state

There are three relevant versions of the project:

| Location | State | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| `main` at `a66995c` | Clean; matches `origin/main`; recent CI green | Stable code base, but its status documents are stale |
| [`wave9/bp31-ladder` PR #45](https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/PointStream/pull/45) | Open, clean, CI green; 16 commits ahead and 7 behind `origin/main` | Contains the newest runner fixes and BP31 evidence |
| `plans/span-result-fold-in` at `0dff035` | Local-only, one commit beyond main | Contains the most accurate current plan, but is not backed up remotely |

So “latest” is split: code and findings are on the Wave 9 branch, while the newest interpretation and next steps are on the local plans branch.

The main handoff currently points to `plans/BP31-findings.md`, but that file exists only in the Wave 9 worktree. Meanwhile [PLAN.md](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/PLAN.md:33) still says Phase B is unmerged, the pipeline does not exist, and BP24 is unfinished—none of which is current. [HANDOFF.md](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/HANDOFF.md:18) also predates the span results.

The other unmerged branches are mostly old Claude work, superseded prototypes, or already protected with archive tags. The HNeRV and FVD branches may contain reusable experiments, but the HNeRV implementation is a lightweight local approximation, depends on deleted pre-rewrite modules, and should not be presented as a credible modern learned-codec baseline.

## What is genuinely strong

The project has several valuable, submission-grade foundations:

- A modular end-to-end runner with contracts and configurable component axes.
- Real coded-rate measurement rather than proxy bit counts.
- Carefully calibrated regional metrics and null controls.
- A useful headroom experiment over eight matches.
- Evidence that corrective residuals can produce favorable incremental tradeoffs in selected short-span cases.
- Good research hygiene: failed assumptions and broken instruments are recorded rather than hidden.
- Healthy ordinary CI: linting, typing, and default tests are green.
- A serious and unusually broad literature review.

This work is worth preserving even if the eventual paper thesis changes.

## The critical scientific gaps

The latest evidence in [BP31 findings](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream-w9-a/plans/BP31-findings.md:516) changes the roadmap materially:

- Multi-scene streaming had not previously completed through the runner; the fix is only on PR #45.
- `background.codec` is ignored in stream mode. `stream_codec` and CRF are the actual controls.
- `BackgroundArtifact.codec` reports the unused sidecar codec, so provenance can be misleading.
- `intra_qp` is unreachable.
- Cross-scene AV1 streaming helps by roughly 19 BD-rate points, but leaves PointStream at **+90.97% BD-rate**.
- PointStream takes approximately **19.1–19.7×** the anchor’s wall-clock time.
- At the actual roughly 43 dB operating point, replacing JPEG with AV1/VVC intra saves only about 31% of plate bytes—not the previously expected 3.6–4.1×.
- Moving from 8 to 16 frames improves the PointStream/AV1 byte ratio only from 2.17× to 2.01×.
- The two-point marginal estimate is about 9,319 bytes/frame for PointStream versus 4,757 for AV1.
- Longer `panorama-stream` runs fail because scene canvases have different sizes.
- Both span runs trigger quality-drift alarms of more than 5 dB.

Consequently, I would not spend the next week primarily optimizing the plate codec. Existing evidence says the next question is where the continuing per-frame cost comes from: residual, crops, object representation, metadata, or some combination.

Other submission blockers remain:

- The central ablation lattice has not been run.
- The perceptual BD-rate implementation needs typed handling of metric direction and units.
- There is no independent second domain.
- There is no credible modern learned-video-codec comparison.
- All attempted generative engines currently lose to a pasted keyframe; generation is disabled in the main ladder.
- The all-off lattice corner is still a shortcut rather than a genuine compositional configuration.
- ROI controls and required-behaviour coverage are incomplete.

## Measurement and reproducibility concerns

I ran the invariant suite separately because [pytest.ini](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/pytest.ini:1) excludes invariants, integration tests, and slow tests by default.

It completed successfully but printed 27 historical runs as uncitable. The suite remains green because [the reporting test](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/tests/invariants/test_outputs_tree.py:72) prints offenders without asserting. More importantly, several custom reports cited by the paper do not carry the standard `invariant_failures` field, and BP21 still contains unresolved or unreclassified bound alarms.

Before submission, every cited report should carry a common manifest:

- Git revision and complete command/configuration
- Input manifest and relevant hashes
- Encoder binary paths and versions
- Predeclared bounds and null controls
- Open alarms and explicitly closed alarms with reasons
- A final machine-readable citability verdict
- Rate, quality, encode time, decode time, and sample count

The paper also cites an `outputs/bp17-baseline/` location that is absent from the configured results root.

## Manuscript assessment

The paper repository is clean and synchronized, but the manuscript is not merely “waiting for results.”

The title still promises [“Live Video Streaming”](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/67a9ea6275d3d9785ce57026/main.tex:42), despite the current runtime. The introduction says the fallback ensures PointStream is never worse than AV1 and claims high-fidelity generative reconstruction and significant bandwidth savings; these are not established. See [introduction.tex](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/67a9ea6275d3d9785ce57026/sections/introduction.tex:6).

Other manuscript issues include:

- A 403-word abstract with no actual result.
- No conclusion.
- Evaluation still structured around holes and expected experiments.
- Generalization prose claims repetitions that have not happened.
- “Two profiles” are described as evaluated when they were not.
- The earlier claim that the plate is the entire cause now conflicts with BP31.
- The abstract promises release of a dataset that appears to include footage with potentially restricted redistribution rights.
- The body has approximately 9,900 words, but very few result visuals; the appendix material is already around 4,300 words and seven tables.

I could not produce an exact page count because no rendered PDF or LaTeX toolchain is present. The TOMM author guide currently states a limit of **23 pages including references**, with up to **five appendix pages in the same PDF**, and encourages supplementary multimedia. The present appendix is likely to be tight once rendered. [ACM TOMM submission guide](https://tomccap.hosting.acm.org/guide.html)

## What I would do next

I would replace the broad roadmap with a short scientific decision gate.

1. Reconcile the repository immediately.

   Merge or otherwise preserve `plans/span-result-fold-in`, update PR #45 against main, and create one authoritative status page. Do not leave the only current interpretation on a local-only branch.

2. Spend three to five days answering whether a viable claim exists.

   - Run `panorama-full` at spans 24, 32, and 48.
   - Split marginal cost into residual, crops, object metadata, and other payloads.
   - Measure quality by frame index and close the current drift alarm.
   - Repair perceptual BD-rate and examine the genuinely low-rate regime with calibrated VMAF/LPIPS, while retaining PSNR and qualitative examples.
   - Repeat the decisive comparison on at least one independent standard sequence.
   - Include the object-stream-off/null configuration.

3. Set a hard go/no-go criterion.

   If no measured crossover or credible winning regime appears—and the best result remains substantially above the anchor—activate the architecture-change branch immediately. Further plate micro-optimization is unlikely to erase a roughly 91% system gap.

4. Only after that decision, fund the full paper campaign.

   That includes the load-bearing lattice ablations, multiple videos, a second domain, a modern learned-codec baseline, full timing, qualitative figures/video, alarm closure, and a complete manuscript rewrite.

If a winning regime is found, the paper should name it narrowly and report how it was found. If none is found honestly, I would delay or retarget rather than force a positive codec claim from a strong experimental framework and negative result.

## What I need clarified

Three decisions materially affect the plan:

- Is September 30 a hard external deadline, or an internal target? I did not find that date in the TOMM submission guide.
- If the decision gate finds no winning regime, are you willing to delay or change the paper’s central thesis?
- Do you have redistribution rights for the curated video corpus? If not, the abstract’s dataset-release promise needs to become a release of annotations, indices, code, and reproducible acquisition instructions.

This review was read-only; I did not change branches, files, worktrees, or results.

Implemented in [draft PR #82](https://github.com/emanuele-artioli/PointStream/pull/82), with new regression tests still awaiting approval.

The implementation includes:

- **Quiet monitoring:** detached execution, timestamped logs, actual-progress tracking, quiet hours, one-shot/hourly reports, and persistent events. Due events are combined into one agent wakeup.
- **Bounded codec adaptation:** short pilots → bounded QP/JPEG spacing adjustments → longer-clip confirmation → final runs. Invalid evidence, exhausted budgets, or unresolved spacing stop advancement.
- **Usage and training guidance:** documented in the [long-job workflow](/tmp/pointstream-long-jobs/docs/workflow/long-jobs.md).

Existing tests, lint, type checking, and architecture checks pass. A detached host smoke run completed, and Codex accepted a queued transport check. Scheduled wakeup from an idle task still needs verification. CI has not appeared yet. Existing jobs and host rules remain unchanged.

**Your training progression is useful, with one additional stage: cross-video validation before final selection.**

| Stage | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Fit and reconstruct one scene | Check that learning and conditioning work; diagnose failures |
| Train on one video, hold out a scene | Check generalization beyond memorized frames |
| Train on diverse development subsets, hold out a development video | Screen for transfer to unseen content |
| Freeze the recipe, train on the eight development videos, evaluate on the two untouched test videos | Final evaluation |

The first stage should **not rank candidates for generalization**. A model that memorizes fastest may generalize poorly. Give candidates meaningful minimum budgets and extend ambiguous cases rather than automatically eliminating half. Group splits by original source or match to avoid leakage between related videos.

For PointStream, rank candidates by their effect on the **complete codec**: transmitted bytes at a quality target, encoding/decoding time, and temporal fidelity. A better-looking generator can still require more residual bits.

There is no demonstrated single best selection method for PointStream. Established approaches include [Hyperband](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v18/16-558.html) for staged budgets and [FABOLAS](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v54/klein17a.html) for dataset-size-based screening. More recent [freeze-thaw optimization](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/rakotoarison24a.html) uses learning curves to allocate further training. Current [DCVC-UF training](https://github.com/microsoft/DCVC/blob/main/training.md) also progressively increases sequence length and patch size. For ten heterogeneous candidates, I recommend transparent staged gates first.

The training protocol is documented; **the retired training evaluator has not been repaired**.

May I add the regression tests covering reporting schedules, stalls, restart/delivery, budgets and promotion, bounded spacing, and invalid results?

The [test-design skill](/home/itec/emanuele/.agents/skills/test-design/SKILL.md) requires “Write only the approved tests.” That approval is the remaining user-input gate; I found no host or PointStream rule conflict requiring a policy change.

finalAnswer.text:
**I recommend keeping ten-minute logging, making chat reports optional and scheduled, and reviewing results before launching each expensive stage.** These are three separate jobs and should have separate policies.

Your existing system has pieces of this, but it does not yet provide a working general adaptive controller. I inspected the current checkout; I haven’t changed rules or the running job.

**What exists today**

- The [host rule](/home/itec/emanuele/.agent-rules/AGENTS.md:237) requires hourly checkpoints and a progress line every ten minutes. It does **not** require ten-minute chat reports.
- The runner’s [heartbeat](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/src/pipeline/dag/heartbeat.py:1) prints “still running” with elapsed time. Redirecting that output to a file needs no model involvement. However, it proves the heartbeat thread is alive—not that useful work is advancing.
- The [low-rate sweep](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/experiments/tier/low_rate_sweep.py:451) supports stages, saved results, resuming, and alarms. It follows predefined points; it does not adjust the next stage based on quality spacing.
- The [training campaign](/home/itec/emanuele/pointstream/scripts/train_campaign.py:1) implements successive halving: small initial budgets, evaluation, pruning, then larger budgets. **Its evaluator currently raises an error because that evaluation path was retired**, so this needs repair before use.

I cannot establish exactly why last night’s task kept reporting without inspecting that task, but the shared ten-minute rule does not demand it.

**Reporting choices**

| Approach | Token use | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| Log only; inspect when wanted | No model tokens for logging | You must check progress yourself |
| Log plus morning/hourly digest | Model runs at report times | Predictable updates; problems may wait until the next report |
| Script monitors health; agent wakes for reports or decisions | Model runs only when useful | Best balance, but requires a small controller |
| Agent checks every ten minutes but stays silent | Still consumes model tokens | Reduces messages without solving the underlying cost |

**The key saving is fewer model invocations, not merely shorter or hidden reports.**

At launch, the agent could ask once for your reporting preference, reusing any preference you already supplied. Your example can be stored as:

> Log progress every ten minutes. Send one digest in eight hours and ask for the next reporting schedule. Until I answer, keep logging without recurring chat reports.

“Now every hour” would update the schedule without restarting the job. Store the actual next-report timestamp and timezone, so resuming a task does not restart the eight-hour countdown.

Scheduled tasks can provide the reporting layer, though tasks needing local files require the computer and app to remain running. The detached GPU job should remain independent of that scheduler. [Official scheduled-task documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/automations?surface=app).

**Adaptive execution should happen at stage boundaries**

Running cheap experiments first is useful when their results can change what runs next. Merely sorting a fixed queue by runtime does not provide that benefit.

For codec ladders, I suggest:

1. Run a small representative pilot with widely separated operating points.
2. Check that the controls actually move size and quality, and record runtime.
3. If qualities cluster, distinguish an ineffective control, metric saturation, or uncertainty from genuinely narrow spacing.
4. Test revised spacing cheaply before committing to slower encodes.
5. Launch the expensive stage from a saved, revised plan.

A fast encoder preset may not predict a slow preset perfectly, so retain a small confirmation probe at the slower setting. Also, similar quality can still be useful if bitrate or runtime differs substantially.

For training, use short initial budgets and checkpoint evaluation across candidates. Run cheap candidates early, but give slower models a minimum meaningful budget: otherwise the procedure can eliminate models that learn slowly but eventually do better. Extend ambiguous cases rather than mechanically pruning half.

Every decision should record the evidence, configuration changes, and remaining compute budget. Keep exploratory tuning separate from the final evaluation set.

**How much autonomy to allow**

| Mode | Behavior | Main tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| Review between stages | Stops for your decision | Simple and controllable; GPU may idle overnight |
| **Bounded adaptation — recommended** | Adjusts spacing, extends uncertain trials, or drops clear losers within agreed limits | Saves compute without requiring constant attention; needs explicit decision rules |
| Open-ended agent supervision | Agent invents follow-up experiments | Flexible, but token cost and search scope become less predictable |

For overnight work, bounded adaptation could continue within an agreed GPU-hour budget, then pause at an unresolved scientific decision and include it in the morning digest. Health checks can still run frequently in ordinary code.

I would implement this in two steps: first clarify the host rule to separate **logging, reporting, and analysis**, with log-only as the fallback; then add stage-boundary decisions to the sweep runner and repair checkpoint evaluation. That addresses the token waste immediately while building toward useful unattended experimentation.

userMessages.text:
We keep trying to improve pointstream but the results are not satisfactory. Let's start from the basics: the idea of this paper is that traditional codecs waste resources because they don't know what they are encoding, so they have to rely on pixel level compression techniques: DCT, residuals, etc., while humans process visual information much more efficiently, by having mental images of common objects, how they move, etc. so we want to leverage thi semantic knowledge to increase video encoding effiency.



From this idea, we derived that a video is composed of background, which the viewer doesn't look at nor cares about very much, and just needs to be encoded good enough to not distract, and foreground, which is more important to encode well. So we wrote the presley paper (/home/itec/emanuele/presley/68e8b6bb11d0dd9e62a67aef) to compress the background more than the foreground, which gets good results.



To push further, we noticed that for example moving humans are complex for a pixel-level codex to compress, but their movement can be easily modeled by computer vision algorithms, for example by tracking their skeleton keypoints. And we wanted to use this for a new compression algorithm for human motion. So we wrote the genstream paper (/home/itec/emanuele/genstream/682c320f388146ae7ee133b7) to show that compressing an ice skating video where the athlete and the background are known in advance, like at the olympics, is a matter of skeleton keypoints and camera poses, which dramatically reduces bitrate compared to streaming a traditional video.



We then set out to extend this idea to more general tasks, where the background is not available in advance as a 3d model, and we noticed that for many content types, for example sports (but also maybe egocentric video and aerial shots), background is not only less crucial to the viewer, but also slow-changing or anyway composed of a static plate that a camera pans, zooms and tilts around. Traditional codecs need to re-encode the background every segment, and even inside the segment, if the camera moves away from a portion of the background, then returns later, the codec might have to re-encode that portion anew, even though its information is available in a previous frame. So we set out to encode the background as a static plate, with panorama stitching algorithms, and saving the warping matrices, which are invertible and thus allow to reobtain the original frames from the panorama, basically consituting a background encoder. The viewer would lose information about how the background changed over time, but save rate at comparable quality.



We identified tennis point scene as a best case scenario, where two athletes holding rackets are moving in the foreground, without overlapping (which complicates the computer vision tasks of detecting them, their shape, and their skeleton keypoints precisely), and a small ball is dashing between them. The background it also the same for a very long time (hours of a match) and static aside from movements from the audience or ball kids, which are not very relevant. The camera is also mostly static, and only panning and zooming. Our assumption is that leveraging these idiosyncrasies supposedly allows a much higher compression efficiency than traditional streaming, so we set out to implement pointstream, merging the genstream approach to human keypoint compression, with the idiosyncrasies of tennis backgrounds.



So then we needed a model that takes a reference image plus skeleton motion, and turns that into a video of the reference image. We first found [https://huggingface.co/lllyasviel/sd-controlnet-openpose](https://huggingface.co/lllyasviel/sd-controlnet-openpose), which does a seemingly correct but rough job, and has no temporal dimension, so every generation risks being very different from the previous one. We looked into and trained various architectures, from SPADE, to multi-controlnets that use segmentations and canny filters, and finally found [https://github.com/HumanAIGC/AnimateAnyone](https://github.com/HumanAIGC/AnimateAnyone), which seems pretty good from the advertisement and demo, so we have also fine tuned that for tennis. We have kept looking for newer, better models, but found nothing better yet. A possible, untested alternative is MTTF: [https://github.com/\](https://github.com/)xyzysz/Extreme-Human-Video-Compression-with-MTTF](https://github.com/]\(https://github.com/\)xyzysz/Extreme-Human-Video-Compression-with-MTTF). It still compresses keyframes with VVC and generates the inter frames. Reportedly, it does beat VVC on talking faces and moving-body clips, at ultra-low rate, with perceptual as well as objective scores. Broadcast tennis at a PSNR ledger is outside that regime: arbitrary clothing, a racket, a ball, 4K texture. Score Pointstream at ultra low rate, where baselines can't do a good job, with a perceptual metric on the player and a geometric check on the court (line alignment). PSNR or VMAF will keep punishing a deliberately soft crowd and will hide a sharp court.



Unfortunately, surpassing vvc and av1 baselines has proven very difficult for several reasons that we have recorded in detail in the documentation of the project. One that might not have been recorded yet is that each scene paid a new background and appearance crop set, but in theory we don't need the appearance vector for each scene, we can send one appearance and one background at the beginning of the match, and use them for the rest of the match, as they should remain the same while the traditional codecs re-encode them at every segment, drastically reducing bitrate of every following match point to the motion keypoints plus residuals. However, today we found out that VVC and AV1 have "composite long-term reference": The encoder builds one extra picture that is never displayed. Blocks are chosen by a combined cost so that still background is kept and moving foreground is left out, often by blending the clean parts of several frames. That picture is inserted as a long-term reference. Later frames predict from it with ordinary block motion compensation and still send a residual. This is the same background idea as PointStream’s plate, which means we cannot just present it as an advantage over baselines, pretending they couldn't do the same. So we should acknowledge the feature, allow baselines to use it, and should evaluate whether to borrow its strengths into pointstream:

1. Most background blocks stay cached for the match; a block is replaced only when lighting or a ball kid has made it stale. That avoids the bitrate burst of restitching the plate.
2. Combined-cost selection, or a mask, is what keeps the player out of the background picture.



So I asked a Cursor session for advice, and it responded:

1. What the idea got right, and where it stops: The chain from Presley to GenStream to PointStream is coherent. Presley showed that a conventional codec spends a disproportionate share of its bits on a small salient region. GenStream showed that if the decoder already has the athlete and the scene, pose and camera replace the pixel stream. PointStream asked whether that second result survives when the background is not a pre-shared 3D model and the athlete is not a pre-shared renderer. It does not, on broadcast tennis, against VVC, at the quality you are scoring. That is a result, not a failure to finish the implementation.
2. Two different bets got bundled into one codec, and only one of them is real.
   1. Rate allocation is real, and it is modest. Painting the players out and re-encoding saves about 14–18% BD-rate on eight 4K scenes (up to about 27% when the player is large, near zero when the player is small and the camera is fast). That saving *is* the player’s bitrate. Putting the player back at the same quality spends it again. You beat the anchor only if the player comes back for less than those bits. On the 23 September background campaign, the only clip that leaves a usable budget at a matched court is Perricard scene 002: the inpainted video is 86,894 bytes against a 104,482 byte source, so 17,588 bytes remain and the foreground only has to match the anchor’s 24.9 dB. Alcaraz scene 000, nearly still, leaves about 40 kB on a panorama with the court 1.5 dB down, and the foreground has to gain about 0.65 dB. Federer scene 007, the clip the ladder has been living on, leaves 4 kB once the court is matched. A small player plus a pan is the worst case for this idea, and it has been the development clip.
   2. The panorama is not a better background model than VVC. A registered plate on Federer sits around 23–24 dB in the background. The residual of that warp is 107 kB at QP 46 to reach 29.6 dB, still short of the anchor’s 31.4 dB background, and the plate plus residual already exceeds the 112 kB anchor before the players are added. VVC’s block motion compensation is already “static court, camera moved,” and it is a finer motion model than one homography: lens distortion, non-planar stands, audience, ball kids. MPEG-4 sprite coding found the same limit twenty years ago. A single mosaic wins when the camera is still or the warp is nearly exact; it loses once perspective error accumulates, which is why later work split sequences into multi-sprites. The “hours of a match” amortization does not rescue this. The plate is a few tens of kilobytes once. The warp residual is about as large as the entire anchor *per 48 frames*. Paying it every frame never amortizes.
3. Of the 136,228 bytes for one crop plus COCO-17, the keypoints are 4,794 bytes: 47 frames times 102 bytes of raw float16. The crop is 1,962 bytes. About 129 kB is the background plate. Pose is 3.5% of the wire. A couple of pixels of lossy error, and a delta from frame t to frame t+1, can shrink those 4,794 bytes toward 1 kB. That is worth doing, and it does not change the comparison. Deleting the pose stream entirely still leaves a bitstream larger than the VVC anchor, because the plate is the bitstream.
4. The registered-plate experiment treated everything behind the players as one layer. A warped sprite reached about 23.6 dB on that whole background. The residual that pulled it toward the anchor was 107 kB and still short of VVC’s 31.4 dB background, at a total already above the 112 kB anchor. Most of that error is not the court plane. Stands, crowd, ball kids, and shadows are not a plane, so one homography cannot lock them. Judging the warp by full-background PSNR made a good court fit look like a bad background model. Instead, the video can be split into multiple layers:
   1. Class 1, the players: One appearance plus body pose plus two or three racket points (hand, throat, tip). The generator’s job is to move that photographed person. The gap is that the generators you have, including the tennis fine-tune of AnimateAnyone, were not trained to read a throat and a tip, so a racket will still smear until the conditioning includes those points. Pose bytes are already about 5 kB of the old 136 kB stream. Lossy, temporally predicted joints are worth doing, but are unlikely to decide the paper. The sprite and the crowd layer will.
   2. Class 2, the court: On a planar court seen by a fixed-mount camera, a homography is the exact frame-to-frame map, including zoom, as long as the camera center does not translate. A cylinder is the right sprite surface for a horizontal pan: a flat mosaic spends its pixels on stretched corners once the pan is wide, which is the cost Farin cut by splitting sprites. OpenCV’s CylindricalWarper builds that piece. A new sprite when the court warp error jumps is the same rule as his partition. PlaneWarper is what you have now; it is the short-pan special case. Estimate that matrix on a cleaned frame, then apply it to the original pixels. Masking people out of the fit is required, or a player step drags the court. Blurring grass grain before the fit keeps the estimate on the lines and the surface contrast. Undistort first when you have the lens; a long broadcast lens is a small correction, a full-court wide view is not. The sprite is built from the original frames. The only allowed generative step on this layer is a seam cleanup after the warp, not a new court. The ball stays on this layer. A trajectory is a few bytes if the detector holds. A residual is a small window around the ball when it does not. The court residual has to be measured on the court mask alone. If that residual is still tens of kilobytes per point, the cylinder did not lock the plane and another warper will not either. If it is small, the previous 107 kB figure was the crowd, and class 3 is allowed to look soft.
   3. Class 3, everyone else: Umpire, ball kids, line judges, crowd, and stands move or sit off the court plane. One blurred plate, warped by the same camera update as the court, is the cheap version, and it is the right default. A coarse temporal stream is the version you use where that plate is visibly wrong. Generating class 3 at the client side, instead of sending it, saves bits only when done at the once at the start of the match, then gets the same warp as the court.
5. A PSNR win against VVC on a 48-frame 4K window is not available from this design. The journal claim that is still available is narrower, and it matches the original idea: 
   1. For fixed-mount pan-tilt-zoom sports, cache the court and one appearance per player for the match, and transmit temporally coded pose plus a ball trajectory. Reconstruct the players with a pose-conditioned generator. In the ultra-low-rate band, where AV1 and VVC smear both the player and the court, the reconstruction might be preferred on a perceptual metric, because the court stays sharp and the player stays an identifiable person. That is distinct from talking-head codecs. Those generate the whole frame from a face prior. A hallucinated sweater is acceptable there; a hallucinated court line is not. PointStream’s contribution is the split: geometry that must stay exact is cached, appearance that a generator can carry is posed, and the object neither can represent (the ball) is sent explicitly. Presley is the evidence that the player is where the conventional codec spends a disproportionate rate. GenStream is the evidence that pose replaces pixels once appearance is known. PointStream is the broadcast case, where the scene is not pre-modeled in 3D and the camera is a PTZ.
   2. Publish LPIPS at matched ultra-low rate. The operating point is below the current QP 46 anchor, at a resolution the generator was trained for, composited back onto the court.
   3. Count the court and the appearance once, and plot rate against longer and longer scenes, until the curve crosses the baseline anchor.



Ask me if anything is unclear, then organize all this content into a new document, that we can reference and update later.

These campaigns exist to find that point before the deadline, one stage at a time. The background campaign is finished.
